Enterprise RAG Knowledge Assistant

An end-to-end Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) application built using Python, FastAPI, Streamlit, Ollama, ChromaDB, and Sentence Transformers.

The application enables users to upload PDF documents, extract and index their content, and ask natural-language questions using a locally configured Large Language Model (LLM).

It combines semantic search with LLM-based answer generation to retrieve relevant document information and provide supporting source references.

1. Project Overview

Traditional Large Language Models rely on their training knowledge and may generate inaccurate responses when answering questions about private or domain-specific documents.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this limitation by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge base and supplying it as context to an LLM.

This project demonstrates the implementation of a document-based RAG application using open-source technologies.

Objectives

Build an end-to-end document question-answering application.

Extract text from uploaded PDF documents.

Split extracted text into manageable chunks.

Generate semantic embeddings using Sentence Transformers.

Store and retrieve document embeddings using ChromaDB.

Generate context-grounded responses using Ollama.

Provide source references and supporting passages.

Expose backend functionality through REST APIs.

Develop an interactive user interface using Streamlit.

The model generates an answer based on the retrieved information.

The model generates an answer based on the retrieved information.

A single prompt handles casual conversation, document questions, and unsupported factual questions. There is no greeting classifier or keyword list. Every valid query uses one generation call, including when no documents are indexed or no passages pass the relevance threshold. The prompt directs conversational replies to omit citations and unsupported factual answers to refuse. Only cited sources are returned. Prompt instructions and valid citations do not guarantee factual support.

Relevance Filtering

The service uses cosine distance exclusively and verifies the persisted Chroma collection configuration. A collection using L2, inner product, or an unknown metric is rejected rather than scored incorrectly. Existing collections are never deleted or converted automatically; incompatible collections require a separately created cosine collection and document re-ingestion.

Cosine similarity is 1 - cosine_distance, with range [-1, 1]. Higher similarity ranks first. RELEVANCE_THRESHOLD is a minimum cosine similarity in [0, 1], not a maximum distance: 0.5 accepts distances at most 0.5; 0.7 accepts distances at most 0.3. Filtering and ranking use unrounded scores. API sources retain raw distance and similarity; similarity_percent is rounded for display only. A displayed 90% means cosine similarity 0.9, not a 90% probability of relevance or a correct answer.

The default RELEVANCE_THRESHOLD=0.5 is a starting point, not a universal recommendation. Raise it to require stronger similarity or lower it to admit more passages. Check representative document questions and out-of-context questions when changing it. No automatic per-query rescaling or fallback lowers the threshold. Retrieval defaults to the nearest three chunks; filtering, deduplication, and citation selection can leave fewer than three returned sources. Chroma uses approximate nearest-neighbor search; this application does not add a cross-encoder reranker or hybrid keyword search.

Ollama chat API and generation options

The implementation keeps the existing native Chroma and Ollama clients; LangChain is not required. Ollama honors OLLAMA_BASE_URL and OLLAMA_MODEL, defaults to llama3.2, and uses non-streaming chat at temperature 0.1. Generation temperature affects randomness, not retrieval similarity. The application's retrieval top_k=3 is unrelated to Ollama's token-sampling options.top_k.

Terminal Debug Logs

Set LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG in .env, or set $env:LOG_LEVEL="DEBUG" in PowerShell before starting the backend. Restart the backend after changing the log level.

Debug logs include the full user query, query embedding, Chroma response, chunk IDs and metadata, ranking and filtering decisions, context, Ollama requests and responses (including token counts and timing fields), citation checks, and final API response. Failures include tracebacks. Logs go to the backend terminal, not the Streamlit terminal.

These logs contain private document text and user data. Use them only for local debugging; set LOG_LEVEL=INFO to disable full payload logging. Treat saved terminal output as sensitive.

A text file (sometimes spelled textfile; an old alternative name is flat file) is a kind of computer file that is structured as a sequence of lines of electronic text. A text file exists stored as data within a computer file system.

In operating systems such as CP/M, where the operating system does not keep track of the file size in bytes, the end of a text file is denoted by placing one or more special characters, known as an end-of-file (EOF) marker, as padding after the last line in a text file.[1] In modern operating systems such as DOS, Microsoft Windows and Unix-like systems, text files do not contain any special EOF character, because file systems on those operating systems keep track of the file size in bytes.[2]

Some operating systems, such as Multics, Unix-like systems, CP/M, DOS, the classic Mac OS, and Windows, store text files as a sequence of bytes, with an end-of-line delimiter at the end of each line.[3][page needed] Other operating systems, such as OpenVMS and OS/360 and its successors, have record-oriented filesystems, in which text files are stored as a sequence either of fixed-length records or of variable-length records with a record-length value in the record header.

"Text file" refers to a type of container, while plain text refers to a type of content.

At a generic level of description, there are two kinds of computer files: text files and binary files.[4][page needed]

Data storage

Data storage

A stylized iconic depiction of a CSV-formatted text file
Because of their simplicity, text files are commonly used for storage of information. They avoid some of the problems encountered with other file formats, such as endianness, padding bytes, or differences in the number of bytes in a machine word. Further, when data corruption occurs in a text file, it is often easier to recover and continue processing the remaining contents. A disadvantage of text files is that they usually have a low entropy, meaning that the information occupies more storage than is strictly necessary.

A simple text file may need no additional metadata (other than knowledge of its character set) to assist the reader in interpretation. A text file may contain no data at all, which is a case of zero-byte file.

Encoding
The ASCII character set is the most common compatible subset of character sets for English-language text files, and is generally assumed to be the default file format in many situations. It covers American English, but for the British pound sign, the euro sign, or characters used outside English, a richer character set must be used. In many systems, this is chosen based on the default locale setting on the computer it is read on. Prior to UTF-8, this was traditionally single-byte encodings (such as ISO-8859-1 through ISO-8859-16) for European languages and wide character encodings for Asian languages.

Because encodings necessarily have only a limited repertoire of characters, often very small, many are only usable to represent text in a limited subset of human languages. Unicode is an attempt to create a common standard for representing all known languages, and most known character sets are subsets of the very large Unicode character set. Although there are multiple character encodings available for Unicode, the most common is UTF-8, which has the advantage of being backwards-compatible with ASCII; that is, every ASCII text file is also a UTF-8 text file with identical meaning. UTF-8 also has the advantage that it is easily auto-detectable. Thus, a common operating mode of UTF-8 capable software, when opening files of unknown encoding, is to try UTF-8 first and fall back to a locale
software, when opening files of unknown encoding, is to try UTF-8 first and fall back to a locale dependent legacy encoding when it definitely is not UTF-8.
